title: High bandwidth heterodyne sensing with bulk NV diamond
authors: H. A. M. Taylor, J. P. Duff, L. B. Miller, A. Tritt, M. S. Oldfield, K. Helmerson, M. S. J. Barson
abstract: Developing high performance portable sensors is of significant importance for both terrestrial and satellite communications, with quantum sensors offering potential advantages in sensitivity and bandwidth. The nitrogen vacancy center in diamond is a popular quantum sensing platform for its relative simplicity and wide range of acceptable operating conditions, but suffers a limited instantaneous bandwidth due to the narrow linewidth of the spin resonance. In this work, we first present a magnetic quantum sensing scheme utilizing heterodyne mixing with strong optical and microwave driving, achieving MHz-scale instantaneous bandwidth with a sensitivity of $548 \; \text{pT/}\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ in an active diamond volume of $ 2.5\times 10^{-4} \; \text{mm}^3$ with $2 \times 10^{11}$ NV centers. We then demonstrate expansion of the sensing bandwidth by employing a strong magnetic gradient and many individually modulated microwave control fields, expanding the single resonance bandwidth to 48 MHz with a peak sensitivity of $8.5 \; \text{nT/}\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$.
summary: This paper details an advanced quantum sensing technique using NV centers in diamond to overcome the bandwidth limitations of conventional magnetic resonance measurements. By employing heterodyne mixing with strong optical and microwave driving, the authors achieve MHz-scale bandwidths while maintaining high sensitivity. The methodology integrates theoretical rate equations with complex signal processing to enable wide-band, multiplexed sensing for practical applications.
main_problem: The primary challenge is developing high-performance, portable quantum sensors with significantly increased instantaneous bandwidth beyond the intrinsic limits imposed by the narrow linewidth of the NV spin resonance.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated achieving MHz-scale instantaneous bandwidth using heterodyne mixing and further expanded this using magnetic gradients, reaching a peak sensitivity of 8.5 nT/sqrt(Hz).
method: The work combines theoretical rate equation modeling with experimental demonstrations of heterodyne detection and advanced signal processing techniques like code-division multiplexing.
model_or_system: The physical system is the Nitrogen Vacancy (NV) center in diamond, which acts as the quantum sensor platform. The sensing mechanism relies on Optically-Detected Magnetic Resonance (ODMR) enhanced via heterodyne mixing.
key_observables: Sensitivity (e.g., 548 pT/sqrt(Hz) to 8.5 nT/sqrt(Hz)), Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR), and the instantaneous bandwidth (BW_het).
important_parameters: The bandwidth is governed by the sum of optical ($\Gamma_p$) and microwave control ($\Gamma_{con}$) de-polarization rates; the system is analyzed in regimes where $\Gamma_p \gg \Gamma_1$.
main_assumptions: Key approximations include assuming the dark state degeneracy is lifted by a static magnetic field and approximating the true NV resonance distribution using the ODMR spectrum for ensemble averaging.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the rate dynamics for conventional vs. heterodyne ODMR, show the theoretical SNR dependence on detuning ($\delta$) and control power ($P_{con}$), and detail the multi-channel expansion scheme using QPSK.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the need for high bandwidth sensing, detailing the theoretical framework using rate equations and heterodyne mixing, demonstrating bandwidth enhancement via gradients, and finally showcasing a complex multi-channel multiplexing scheme for wide-band target recovery.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to AMO physics and quantum optics as it pushes the boundaries of quantum sensing by engineering the measurement bandwidth using coherent driving fields (heterodyne mixing) rather than relying solely on intrinsic linewidths.
